en: Homage at all times and in every way to the One who possesses the power of the Ten Powers, the Sovereign of Speech and Mind. Especially homage to the One who is the sole dispeller of all distress within the jewel-mine of saṃsāra—so turbulent with waves of rebirth, filled with floods of many diseases, and teeming with the serpents of various births, deaths, and fierce addictions; to the One whose mouth is selflessness (*nairātmya*), the conqueror of the four Māras, the remover of the net of suffering for the world, the breaker of the knot of existence, the destroyer of the Lord of Death, the uprooter of desire, and the benefactor established in the lineage of the Great Kings, [bestowing grace] upon the entire world.

To the one who beholds all, the teacher of the Eightfold Path, the grateful one, the knower of various languages, the knower of all intentions, the wise one, the treasury of the True Dharma, the great orator, the one whose knowledge is unobstructed and who has extracted the thorns of affliction by means of the scriptures; the one whose mind is not distracted by the charms of the goddess Kāmadharā; the one who embraces all sentient beings with the arms of compassion and loving-kindness; the steadfast, the heroic, the peaceful, the self-controlled, the beloved, the protector, the auspicious one; the one always worshipped by the hosts of gods such as Rudra, Indra, and Viṣṇu; the one of immeasurable power.

To the one of peaceful nature, whose voice is beautiful, clear, profound, and steady; to the peerless and supreme one who is immeasurable; to him whose mind is unperturbed by blame or praise; to the one for whom all streams of the outflows have been severed, yet who is born [in the world].

To him whose lotus-like feet and hands are covered with a web of lines like those on the feet of a swan, and who possesses the splendor of a body marked with auspicious signs such as the jar, thunderbolt, wheel, conch, goad, lotus, fish, banner, and parasol; to him whose shanks are firm like those of a deer, whose seven parts of the body are elevated, whose private organ is concealed within a sheath, whose chest is broad and full, whose upper body is like that of a lion, and whose complexion is indescribable due to the fineness of his skin; to him who steals the beauty of pillars made of refined gold with his graceful majesty.

To him whose two arms were thick, firm, and long; whose faintly visible lines were as red as slightly blossomed *bandhūka* flowers; whose tongue was long, broad, thick, and deep red; whose teeth were closely set, white, long, and glossy; whose pair of eyes was serene, with eyelashes like those of a cow, copper-hued at the edges, gentle, and unblinking, reaching as far as his ears; whose long eyebrows were joined and dark-blue, marked by a tuft of hair (*ūrṇā*); whose hair was curled, glossy, fine, black, growing one by one, and thick; whose head was crowned by a turban (*uṣṇīṣa*); and who possessed the majesty of a lion-king and was full of splendor.

Homage to the Protector, the giver of the reality of ultimate meaning, whose body is adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs—refulgent, peerless, and incomparable; born from the mass of sublime merit accumulated over thousands of millions of great eons; possessing a gentle, wondrous, and inconceivable form produced from the radiance of that merit; and whose hair grows upward in a clockwise curl at the navel.

To him who has realized the ultimate truth, whose mind is permeated by all noble qualities, who has raised the banner of the Dharma through correct proclamation, who has felled the forest of the essence of ignorance; who has proclaimed the holy life (*brahmacarya*) with its own meaning and beautiful phrasing—unbroken, flawless, stainless, and supreme; who establishes others in a state of abiding that is most excellent and blameless; who, as a lord, constantly emits dense masses of light-rays that illuminate the intervals between all worlds; who is eloquent, generous, disciplined, wise, intelligent, modest, and glorious.

To him who regards friend, enemy, and neutral alike; who has crossed over the suffering of the wilderness of saṃsāra; who is perfected and pure; whose power is perfection; who is worthy of offerings; who is free from dualities; who is a caravan leader; whose fame and majesty proclaim his renown throughout the three worlds; who has abandoned ill-spoken words and frequents well-spoken ones; who is free from intoxication and tranquil; who has dried up the river of craving; who has proclaimed the Dharma without the teacher’s closed fist; whose stability exceeds that of Meru and the other kings of mountains; whose mind is as unfathomably deep as the ocean; and who possesses a supreme forbearance like the earth.

Constant salutations to that virtuous man who, speaking with patience, fulfills the hopes of those seeking other things by giving away his children, wife, and even his own mind, according to their desires.

Having praised the Buddha-lotus—with its blossoming petals of compassion, its pericarp of patience, its stalk of ethical conduct, its shimmering filaments of meditative concentration, its pollen of the factors of enlightenment, awakened by its own radiance, anointed with the fragrance of renown, and whose mass of pollen of the True Dharma is sipped by the swarms of virtuous bees—I have acquired merit. By this merit, may all beings be freed from the arising of suffering; and may I always and in every way be seen and heard for the benefit of the entire world.

"Even if he has come merely for conversation, or has been touched by my memory, that handsome one—possessing sovereign power and inexhaustible wisdom, beloved of the preeminent, with a form dear to all beings, of flawless limbs, of noble birth, a master of the arts, a knower of the meaning of all scriptures, with delicate skin, gentle, sweet-voiced, renowned, praiseworthy, illustrious, free from disease, devoted to detachment from sensual desires, his resolute intention embraced by compassion, and remembering his former births—may he never be separated from those he loves, nor [united] with those he dislikes."

May I be a Victor, whose association is always with the virtuous, who takes refuge in them, whose mindfulness inclines toward the Dharma, who is endowed with generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and vigor, joined with meditative concentration and true wisdom, and who, through other methods of the conduct of enlightenment, has completely fulfilled the primary practices rooted in perfect awakening, and who is the sole deliverer from all obstructions.
Thus ends the hymn to the Blessed Buddha composed in the Daṇḍaka meter.
